cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: Who Changed It?
cards.instruction: Ask innocent questions until someone admits altering the plan, schedule, arrangement, or shared space.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: The cupboard won't open. I'll approve this room once we establish whether the sofa was this close yesterday.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Can I keep the extra space for yoga?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Yoga is approved in principle. Did obtaining that space involve moving this sofa?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Yes, I moved it. I put the things you need somewhere easier.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Convenience is approved too. Would those be the mugs in your sock drawer, or is someone else improving the room?

cardFidelity.evidence: A3 approves yoga in principle while asking about the sofa move; A5 approves convenience while probing the admitted relocation of needed items.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 yoga request causes A3 spatial-change question; B4 admitted move and helpful relocation cause A5 a specific mug-location inquiry.

relationship.evidence: B2 seeks useful space and B4 explains efforts to preserve access, making B a plausible improver whose changes have side effects.

heightening.evidence: B4 sofa admission widens to moved contents, so A5 gently asks responsibility for the mugs too.

specificity.evidence: A1 blocked cupboard, B2 yoga space and A5 sock-drawer mugs establish understandable shared-space changes.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 someone-else-improving question is earned by B4 helpful framing and avoids an unrelated accusation.
